newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Austrian far-right argues for lower taxes, jobs.
newsitem.headline: Austrian far-right argues for lower taxes, jobs.

text.p: Austria's far-right Freedom Party, keen to portray itself as a voice of moderation, tried to snatch the economic initiative from the government as it wound up a convention on Sunday.

Some 600 Freedom Party faithful gathered for two days in this western provincial town that has more of the flavour of neighbouring Switzerland than of the Austrian capital some 700 km (400 miles) away.

Populist leader Joerg Haider, re-elected head of Europe's biggest far-right movement by a landslide, presented the Freedom Party's recipe for reviving the Austrian economy against a stage backdrop: "Cut taxes, create jobs".
"We stand for a lean state, low taxes and we support small and medium-sized business," Haider told a packed hall, echoing former British prime minister Margaret Thatcher whom he has said he admires.
He accused the ruling coalition of Social Democrats and conservative People's Party of neglecting ordinary Austrians in their haste to join a planned single European currency.

"Unlike the government, we recognise that our goal has to be the creation of jobs, not achieving the Maastricht (Treaty) criteria," Haider said. "We have to stem the rising tide of company insolvencies and fight unemployment."

The Freedom Party swept to its best election result to date in a European parliamentary poll in October. It snatched 27.6 percent of the vote and came within striking distance of the left-right coalition that has governed Austria for a decade.
The party's biggest inroads were among working class voters, concerned about housing and jobs and unhappy about an influx of foreign labour.
Although Austrian joblessness is low by European standards at just over four percent, in some sectors, notably construction, it has reached a post-World War Two high.
The number of firms filing for insolvency also looks certain to hit a 50-year high this year.

"Only the Freedom Party will make the reforms necessary to secure the Austrian economy, guarantee education and secure social standards while creating new jobs and defending incomes," the party leadership said in a policy document.

It proposed slashing unwieldy government bureaucracy and cutting red tape that it claimed was choking innovation. By reducing industry's tax burden the Freedom Party said it would free up more money for investment.
Income tax should fall to an average 40 percent and eventually 35 percent from around 43 percent now, it argued. The document also backed a clampdown on foreign labour until the job market recovered.
Policy makers put forward a list of sell-off candidates including the nation's two biggest banks Bank Austria and Creditanstalt and a host of prosperous industrial groups.
"The state is an extremely bad business manager," the document said.

Haider has sought to claim the centre ground of Austrian politics during the two-day conference and chose Susanne Riess-Passer, a 35-year-old journalist, as party manager in a bid to appeal to more women voters.
